column1: State the Handshaking Lemma formula relating vertex degrees to edge count.
column2: $$\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2|E|$$ Each edge contributes exactly 1 to the degree of each of its two endpoints, so summing degrees counts every edge twice.

column1: What immediate corollary follows from the Handshaking Lemma regarding odd-degree vertices?
column2: The number of vertices with odd degree is always even, since the total degree sum $2|E|$ is even, forcing the odd-degree terms to pair up.

column1: Differentiate a simple graph, multigraph, and pseudograph.
column2: A simple graph forbids loops and multiple edges. A multigraph permits multiple edges between the same vertex pair. A pseudograph additionally permits loops (which contribute 2 to a vertex's degree).

A walk is a vertex sequence $v_0,\dots,v_k$ with consecutive vertices adjacent. A path is a walk with no repeated vertices. A cycle is a closed walk ($v_0=v_k$) where all intermediate vertices are distinct.

column1: Distinguish weak connectivity from strong connectivity in directed graphs.
column2: Weakly connected: the underlying undirected graph (ignoring edge direction) is connected. Strongly connected: every ordered pair of vertices $(u,v)$ has a directed path from $u$ to $v$, respecting edge orientation.

column1: Why is 'is strongly connected to' an equivalence relation among vertices in a digraph, but strong connectivity partitions vertices differently than weak connectivity?
column2: Two vertices $u,v$ are defined strongly connected if directed paths exist both from $u$ to $v$ and $v$ to $u$; this relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, so it partitions $V$ into strong components — but these components can be proper subsets of weak components since direction restricts reachability.

column1: What is the exact edge count of a tree on $n$ vertices, and why is this threshold forced?
column2: A tree has exactly $n-1$ edges. Starting from $n$ isolated vertices, each edge added reduces the component count by exactly 1, so $n-1$ edges are needed to reach a single connected component; any additional edge must join already-connected vertices, creating a cycle.

column1: List the six mutually equivalent characterizations of a tree on $n$ vertices.
column2: (i) Connected and acyclic. (ii) Connected with $|E|=n-1$. (iii) Acyclic with $|E|=n-1$. (iv) Unique simple path between every vertex pair. (v) Minimally connected (removing any edge disconnects it). (vi) Maximally acyclic (adding any edge creates exactly one cycle).

column1: In the tree characterization proof, how is the uniqueness of simple paths (property iv) derived from connectivity and acyclicity (property i)?
column2: Assume two distinct simple paths $P_1,P_2$ exist between $u$ and $v$. They must diverge at some vertex $w$ along different edges and reconverge at some vertex $z$; combining the diverging and reconverging segments forms a cycle, contradicting acyclicity. Hence the path must be unique.

column1: What key data-structure difference distinguishes DFS from BFS, and what does each guarantee?
column2: DFS uses a stack (explicit or recursive call stack) to explore as deep as possible before backtracking, useful for cycle detection and topological ordering. BFS uses a queue to explore vertices in increasing order of distance from the source, guaranteeing shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

column1: What invariant does graph traversal maintain regarding vertex discovery, and what structural information does discovery order encode?
column2: Each vertex transitions from undiscovered to discovered exactly once during traversal; the order of discovery encodes information used to determine distances, articulation points, bridges, and cycle membership.

column1: Why does equivalence relation structure (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) guarantee that connected components partition the vertex set $V$ of an undirected graph?
column2: Reachability via paths is reflexive (empty path to self), symmetric (reverse the path), and transitive (concatenate paths), satisfying the equivalence relation axioms; equivalence relations always partition their underlying set into disjoint equivalence classes, which here are the connected components.
